batchName: Late Republic: Caesar in Gaul (58-50 BCE) - Hard Batch 1
chapterName: Late Republic: Caesar in Gaul (58-50 BCE)

questions.question: Roughly how far did a single legion's baggage train stretch on the march?
questions.explanation: A legion needed around a thousand pack animals, stretching some 4 km (2.5 miles). Supply was Rome's weak point throughout the war.
questions.sourceQuote: Even so, a legion needed around a thousand pack animals, its baggage train (*impedimenta*), which stretched some 4 km (2.5 miles) on the march.

questions.question: When did Gaul finally become formal Roman provinces?
questions.explanation: Gaul was organised into provinces only in 27 BC, under Rome's first emperor. Its Latin later grew into French.
questions.sourceQuote: Gaul became formal provinces only in 27 BC, under Rome's first emperor, and its Latin later grew into French.

questions.question: After the Nervii were beaten in 57 BC, the Senate voted Caesar a record-length public thanksgiving. How long was it?
questions.explanation: The 15-day thanksgiving was the longest yet. It followed a near-disaster in which the Nervii ambushed the legions while they were building camp.
questions.sourceQuote: The Senate later voted him a 15-day public thanksgiving (*supplicatio*), the longest yet.

questions.question: Which goods did the prosperous Gallic tribes trade for Roman wine? (select all that apply)
questions.explanation: The Gauls traded grain, iron and slaves for Roman wine, and they minted their own coins. Their wealth made Gaul a tempting target for conquest.
questions.sourceQuote: They minted coins and traded grain, iron and slaves for Roman wine.

questions.question: Since when have scholars become markedly sceptical of Caesar's account of the Gallic War?
questions.explanation: Until the 20th century scholars largely trusted Caesar's Commentaries. His claims of over a million Gauls killed and almost no Roman dead have fuelled the doubts.
questions.sourceQuote: Since the Second World War they have grown sceptical.

questions.question: What does archaeology suggest about Caesar's siege lines at Alesia?
options: They lay well away from Mont Auxois
They were less continuous than Caesar claimed, but held
They never existed and were invented by Caesar
They were built of stone rather than earth
They were breached by the relief army
They were twice as long as Caesar described
questions.explanation: The lines had gaps Caesar didn't mention, yet they did their job. They included ditches, ramparts, towers and hidden pits with fire-hardened stakes.
questions.sourceQuote: Archaeology suggests the lines were less continuous than Caesar claimed, but they held.

questions.question: What made Caesar's war against the king of the Suebi politically awkward?
options: He had helped Rome against the Helvetii
He was married to a daughter of Pompey
He held Roman citizenship through Crassus
The Aedui had sworn to defend him
He had paid tribute to Rome for a decade
The Senate had named him a friend of Rome the year before
questions.explanation: Only a year earlier the Senate had declared this Germanic king a friend of Rome. Caesar attacked after Gallic allies complained of the king's conquests.
questions.sourceQuote: Only the year before, the Senate (*senatus*) had named this king a friend of Rome.

questions.question: What had happened to Vercingetorix's father?
options: He fell in battle against the Suebi
He was exiled by the druids
He was killed by his own people for trying to make himself king
He died fighting Caesar at Bibracte
He was poisoned by rival Aeduan nobles
He was executed by Roman order
questions.explanation: His father, a nobleman, was killed for seeking kingship. Vercingetorix himself was later proclaimed king after driving out pro-Roman nobles.
questions.sourceQuote: His father, a nobleman, had been killed by his own people for trying to make himself king.

questions.question: How did Caesar's enemies in the Senate react to his massacre of two peoples near the Rhine in 55 BC?
options: They sent envoys to apologise to the Germans
They praised it as a defensive victory
They ordered him to return to Rome
They stripped him of two legions
questions.explanation: Caesar fell on an undefended camp, killing men, women and children. His claim of 430,000 dead is impossible, but the massacre was bad enough to prompt calls for prosecution.
questions.sourceQuote: Still, the massacre was bad enough that his enemies in the Senate wanted to prosecute him.

questions.question: Which details describe the siege of the second Roman camp during the winter revolt of 54 BC? (select all that apply)
options: Over 90 per cent of defenders were killed or wounded
Defenders accepted safe passage and left
The camp fell before Caesar arrived
It lasted more than two weeks
Rebels used siege towers built on Roman models
Caesar relieved it by landing troops from the sea
questions.explanation: The rebels copied Roman siege technology and held the camp under attack for over two weeks. Caesar rescued it with forced marches of about 32 km a day, but by then over 90 per cent of its defenders were dead or wounded.
questions.sourceQuote: Rebels then besieged a second camp for more than two weeks, using siege towers built on Roman models.
